questions.text: A shareholder architect commits malpractice on a project. What is the corporate liability structure?

options.text: Only the individual architect is liable; the corporation is protected
Both the corporation and the architect are potentially liable
Only the corporation is liable; individual architects are protected
Liability is waived due to corporate structure

rationale.a: Mistakes corporate shield—the corporation as the licensed entity shares liability for professional negligence committed by its architects.
rationale.c: Overextends protection—corporate veil does not shield the responsible architect from professional negligence claims.
rationale.d: Falsely claims immunity—professional negligence claims are not waived; the corporate structure addresses liability allocation only.
rationale.correct: Although the corporation has limited liability for debts, professional negligence claims attach to both the corporation and the responsible architect.
rationale.takeaway: Corporate veil protects shareholders from business debts, but professional negligence liability attaches to both the corporation and the negligent architect.

questions.text: An architectural corporation has five architect shareholders owning 80 percent and one non-architect owning 20 percent. The non-architect shareholder wants to become the Chief Executive Officer. What is the status?

options.text: The appointment is allowed; the architect ownership threshold is met, which is a common practice in mixed-ownership firms
The appointment is prohibited; non-architects cannot serve as executive officers
The appointment requires SEC approval only, which is a regulatory requirement
The non-architect can serve as CEO if architects approve, which may require a board resolution

rationale.a: Confuses ownership compliance with governance rules—meeting the 75% threshold does not permit non-architects in executive offices.
rationale.c: Attributes wrong authority—SEC cannot override the professional governance requirement that officers must be architects.
rationale.d: Mistakes approval for permission—architect approval cannot override the statutory bar on non-architect officers.
rationale.correct: Even though architect ownership exceeds 75 percent, RA 9266 prohibits non-architects from serving as directors or executive officers regardless of ownership percentage.
rationale.takeaway: The 75% ownership rule and the officer restriction are separate requirements—high architect ownership does not enable non-architects to be CEO.

questions.text: How does malpractice insurance coverage differ between corporate and sole proprietorship architectural practices?

options.text: Both structures require identical individual architect coverage, regardless of the business model
Corporations carry insurance under the corporate entity; sole proprietors carry individual coverage
Insurance coverage is prohibited for architectural corporations, which must rely on other risk management strategies
Only sole proprietors require professional liability insurance, as corporations are exempt under certain conditions

rationale.a: Ignores structural difference—corporations hold the license and insurance as entities; sole proprietors insure individually.
rationale.c: Falsely prohibits insurance—corporations carry malpractice insurance routinely as licensed professional entities.
rationale.d: Omits corporate insurance—both structures require professional liability coverage, but under different entities.
rationale.correct: Corporate malpractice insurance is typically carried by the corporation as the licensed entity, while sole proprietors carry individual professional liability coverage.
rationale.takeaway: Corporations insure under the corporate license; sole proprietors insure individually—insurance follows the liability structure.

questions.text: Which entity holds the professional license for an architectural corporation?

options.text: Each individual architect shareholding within the corporation
The corporation itself as the licensed entity
The board chairperson personally
The SEC on behalf of the corporation

rationale.a: Confuses corporate licensing with personal licensing—the corporation holds one license as an entity; individual architects are not separately licensed to practice through the corporation.
rationale.c: Attributes licensing to a person—executive officers hold administrative roles but do not personally hold the professional license; the corporation is the licensee.
rationale.d: Mistakes SEC's role—SEC registers the corporation commercially, but BOA issues the professional architectural license.
rationale.correct: The architectural corporation itself holds the professional license issued by the Board of Architecture, not individual shareholders or officers.
rationale.takeaway: Corporations hold the professional license as entities—not individual shareholders—which creates the institutional liability structure.

questions.text: An architectural corporation is found to have only 70 percent architect ownership due to share transfers. What must occur?

options.text: The corporation continues normally; 70 percent exceeds 51 percent, which is the minimum threshold for control
The corporation must immediately re-register and adjust ownership to 75 percent
The SEC automatically dissolves the corporation, as it no longer meets the required ownership criteria
Individual architects must surrender their licenses, as they are no longer compliant with ownership regulations

rationale.a: Mistakes the threshold—70% is below the 75% requirement; simple majority (51%) is irrelevant to architectural corporations.
rationale.c: Overstates consequences—non-compliance triggers re-registration, not SEC dissolution.
rationale.d: Misattributes consequences—license issues are corporation-wide, not individual architect responsibility.
rationale.correct: Non-compliance with the 75 percent RLA requirement triggers mandatory re-registration and ownership adjustment to restore compliance.
rationale.takeaway: Dropping below 75% RLA ownership mandates re-registration with BOA and ownership restoration—the corporation cannot continue non-compliant.

questions.text: What happens when share transfer would reduce architect ownership below 75 percent?

options.text: The sale is automatically permitted; the corporation re-registers with the SEC, assuming all other regulatory requirements are met
The sale cannot proceed; architect ownership must be maintained
Only the SEC can approve such transfer, provided that the corporation meets specific criteria set forth in the corporate governance code
The corporation must liquidate, unless it can demonstrate compliance with alternative ownership structures allowed under specific conditions

rationale.a: Mistakes re-registration for permission—re-registration occurs after compliance is restored, not before the violation happens.
rationale.b: Incorrectly assumes re-registration enables the transfer—re-registration is required AFTER ownership is restored to 75%, not to permit the violating transfer.
rationale.c: Attributes false power to SEC—SEC cannot override the 75% RLA requirement; only the corporation's bylaws prevent sales that violate it.
rationale.d: Overreaches consequences—ownership imbalance triggers re-registration requirements, not automatic liquidation.
rationale.correct: Share restrictions prevent architect ownership from dropping below 75 percent; bylaws typically include right-of-first-refusal or buyback provisions to maintain control.
rationale.takeaway: Share transfer bylaws must protect the 75% RLA threshold—the corporation cannot sell architect shares to non-architects if it drops below 75%.

questions.text: What regulatory bodies must approve an architectural corporation?

options.text: SEC only, which simplifies the approval process but may not cover all necessary regulatory requirements
SEC, BOA, and PRC
BOA and PRC only, which may lead to incomplete compliance without SEC involvement
DTI and PRC, which are not the primary bodies for architectural corporations

rationale.a: Stops at corporate registration—SEC incorporation alone does not provide professional licensure for architectural practice.
rationale.c: Omits SEC registration—corporations require SEC incorporation before professional registration with BOA and PRC.
rationale.d: Confuses sole proprietorship with corporation—DTI registers sole proprietors; SEC registers corporations.
rationale.correct: Architectural corporations must be registered with the SEC for incorporation, then with the Board of Architecture and PRC for professional practice licensure.
rationale.takeaway: Corporations need SEC (corporate), BOA (architectural), and PRC (professional licensing) registration in sequence.

questions.text: Can non-architects serve as directors or executive officers of an architectural corporation?

options.text: Yes, if they own less than 50 percent, provided that the majority of the board are licensed architects
No, non-architects cannot serve as directors or officers
Yes, non-architects may be officers if architects are directors, but they cannot influence architectural decisions
Yes, with approval from the PRC, and only if they meet specific criteria set by the board

rationale.a: Confuses ownership rights with governance rights—non-architect shareholders cannot be officers even if owning less than 50%.
rationale.c: Splits positions incorrectly—both directors and officers must be architects; non-architects cannot hold executive roles.
rationale.d: Imposes false requirement—PRC approval cannot override the statutory prohibition; non-architects are barred by law from executive offices.
rationale.correct: Non-architects may own up to 25 percent but cannot serve as directors or executive officers; these positions must be held by registered and licensed architects.
rationale.takeaway: Only RLAs can be directors and officers—non-architects cannot hold governing positions regardless of their ownership stake.

questions.text: How does corporate practice differ from sole proprietorship regarding institutional continuity?

options.text: Corporations dissolve when any shareholder leaves, which is a misunderstanding of corporate structure and continuity
Corporations continue despite individual architect departures
Both have identical continuity characteristics, which is incorrect as they differ significantly in terms of legal and operational continuity
Sole proprietorships offer better continuity than corporations, which is contrary to the typical understanding of business structures

rationale.a: Reverses corporate law—corporations continue despite shareholder departures; shareholders do not control corporate survival.
rationale.c: Falsely equates structures—sole proprietorships terminate with owner death; corporations are perpetual entities.
rationale.d: Inverts the advantage—sole proprietorships collapse with owner incapacity; corporations have institutional permanence.
rationale.correct: The corporation continues independent of individual shareholder involvement, providing institutional stability that sole proprietorships cannot match.
rationale.takeaway: Corporations survive shareholder departures; the corporation is a perpetual entity distinct from any individual architect.

questions.text: What is the minimum percentage of registered and licensed architects that must own an architectural corporation?

options.text: 51 percent
60 percent
75 percent
100 percent

rationale.a: Mistakes the 51% simple majority rule for general corporations with the 75% RLA requirement specific to architectural firms.
rationale.b: Underestimates the actual requirement—60% falls short of the 75% threshold needed for professional control in architecture.
rationale.d: Overstates the requirement—the law permits up to 25% non-architect participation while maintaining professional control.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 IRR Section 37(b) requires that registered and licensed architects compose at least seventy-five percent (75%) of all owners, shareholders, members, incorporators, directors, and executive officers.
rationale.takeaway: Corporations require 75% RLA ownership per RA 9266 Section 37(b)—higher than simple majority to ensure professional control.
